focus.label: Alcohol-induced ventricular arrhythmia
focus.why: The current frontier 'alcohol-induced arrhythmia' is too broad. The graph shows short-run ventricular tachycardia and high-grade AV block (node-9/node-10), indicating the arrhythmia originates from ventricular or conduction tissue. Alcohol can directly trigger ventricular arrhythmias through sympathetic activation and ion-channel effects, so this is the most direct fine-grained refinement.

payload.report: Recurrent syncope occurring 6-20 hours after heavy alcohol intake, together with ECG showing high-grade AV block, short-run ventricular tachycardia, and extensive ST-segment elevation, points to alcohol-triggered cardiac arrhythmia. Normal troponin and only 10% coronary stenosis exclude acute coronary syndrome and myocardial injury, while absent abdominal, glucose, and neurological evidence makes GI, hypoglycemic, and neural causes unlikely. Among alcohol-induced arrhythmia subtypes, ventricular arrhythmia best explains the clinical episodes and ECG abnormalities, supported by the temporal relationship to alcohol and the absence of fixed coronary disease. Coronary vasospasm, Brugada syndrome, and isolated AV block remain possible but less likely. Pending serum ethanol, Holter monitoring, and echocardiography results temper final certainty, yet the current evidence most strongly supports alcohol-induced ventricular arrhythmia.
